query_text: How much of sexual orientation is innate? Can being gay or straight be societally influenced?

annotations.title: Large-scale GWAS reveals insights into the genetic architecture of same-sex sexual behavior - PubMed

content.text:
**Short answer:** Sexual orientation appears to be **partly innate/biological**, but not determined by a single “gay gene” or one simple cause. Society can strongly influence **how people label themselves, whether they disclose, whom they date or marry, and what behaviors they report**—but there’s little evidence that society can simply make someone gay or straight in the sense of changing their underlying pattern of attraction.

### What “innate” means here

Sexual orientation is usually understood as a pattern of attraction—toward the same sex/gender, another sex/gender, more than one gender, etc. The best evidence suggests it develops through a **complex mix** of factors, including genetics, prenatal biology, and other developmental influences. Large genetic studies have found that genetics contribute somewhat to same-sex sexual behavior, but no genetic profile can reliably predict an individual’s orientation. A major 2019 GWAS of nearly half a million people found several associated genetic loci, but concluded that same-sex sexual behavior is highly polygenic and not explained by one gene. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31467194/?utm_source=openai))

So: **not “born this way” in a simple one-cause sense**, but also **not a voluntary lifestyle choice**.

### Can society influence whether someone is gay or straight?

It depends what you mean by “influence.”

**Society can influence:**

- Whether someone feels safe recognizing or admitting their attractions.
- Whether they identify as gay, straight, bisexual, queer, etc.
- Whether they enter same-sex or opposite-sex relationships.
- Whether they marry, have children, or suppress certain desires.
- How they interpret attractions—e.g., as “bisexual,” “mostly straight,” “curious,” “gay,” or something else.
- Rates of reported same-sex behavior in surveys, because stigma changes what people are willing to report.

**Society probably does not strongly determine the underlying direction of attraction** in the way that, say, cultural fashion determines clothing preference. Professional organizations generally reject the idea that sexual orientation is chosen or can be reliably changed by social pressure or therapy; the Royal College of Psychiatrists, for example, describes orientation as biological in nature and not a choice, while also acknowledging complexity. ([rcpsych.ac.uk](https://www.rcpsych.ac.uk/docs/default-source/members/sigs/rainbow/rainbow-sig-rcpsych-response-human-sexuality.pdf?utm_source=openai))

### What about “environmental influence”?

This is where the word **environment** can be misleading. In behavioral genetics, “environment” does **not necessarily mean society, parenting, media, school, or peer influence**. It can include prenatal hormonal conditions, womb environment, random developmental variation, birth order effects, stressors, and many other non-genetic influences.

So when studies say sexual orientation is influenced by “genes and environment,” that does **not** mean “people become gay because of culture” or “parents/social trends cause it.” The environmental component may be developmental and biological rather than social.

### Is straightness or gayness fixed?

For many people, orientation is quite stable over life. For some, especially people with bisexual or fluid patterns of attraction, labels and attractions may shift over time. But that doesn’t imply people can deliberately choose their orientation. It’s more like handedness, temperament, or certain aspects of personality: biologically influenced, developmentally complex, and not easily changed by willpower.

### Bottom line

A good summary would be:

> Sexual orientation is influenced by biology and development, including genetics, but it is not genetically predetermined in a simple way. Society can shape identity, expression, behavior, and openness, but there is little evidence that society can straightforwardly turn someone gay or straight.

So being gay or straight is **not purely innate in the simplistic “one gene decides it” sense**, but it is also **not merely socially constructed or freely chosen**.
